Nipple trauma

One sham-controlled trial found short-term pain relief after a single laser session, but pooled pain estimates remain uncertain and lesion-healing evidence is sparse.

Publications and records

13publications

Publication and study types

  • Human randomized trials6
  • Human uncontrolled study1
  • Human case series1
  • Systematic reviews and meta-analyses2
  • Protocols3

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Pain during breastfeeding — Gaitero et al. 2025 pooled three randomized trials and reported a mean difference of −0.60 points on the visual analog scale (95% CI −1.52 to 0.31), which is not statistically conclusive.

Sucking pain — Alves et al. 2025 reported an odds ratio of 0.43 in a seven-study review. The published 95% confidence interval has a negative lower bound (−0.23 to 0.79), which is not a valid interval for an odds ratio and requires clarification.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low-to-moderate certainty for short-term pain relief with selected protocols. One sham-controlled study found lower pain through seven days, while other trials were null and the pooled VAS estimate was imprecise (Gaitero et al. 2026; Gaitero et al. 2025).

Low certainty for lesion healing because the clinical studies are small and the reviews use different study sets and measures (Chaves et al. 2012; Alves et al. 2025).

Summary of the Evidence

Thirteen publications are relevant to PBM for nipple pain or injury during breastfeeding: six randomized trials, one uncontrolled treatment study, one case series, two systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and three protocols. The protocols describe planned studies rather than treatment results. The reviews overlap in included trials and assess different outcomes, so they are not independent sets of patient data.

Human and clinical evidence

A double-blind randomized trial of 60 postpartum women found lower pain after one laser session than after sham treatment from 30 minutes through seven days. Satisfaction did not differ, and the report identified no adverse effects (Gaitero et al. 2026).

A 58-participant feasibility trial found no statistically significant between-group differences in clinical outcomes. It was designed to test feasibility rather than efficacy (de Paula Leite et al. 2026).

Earlier results were mixed. A 59-woman trial found lower pain after the first of three daily treatments, whereas a separate single-session randomized trial found no pain reduction (Coca et al. 2016; Camargo et al. 2019).

A 16-woman pilot reported faster lesion healing and less pain, but baseline pain was higher in the treatment group, making the between-group change difficult to interpret (Chaves et al. 2012). A related trial compared PBM with topical cream in 50 women with nipple pain and fissures and reported improvements with PBM after several weeks (Elseody et al. 2024).

A 2025 meta-analysis of three randomized trials found no statistically clear pooled difference in pain. A second 2025 review included seven studies and reported less sucking pain and faster healing, but its reported odds-ratio confidence interval has a negative lower bound and needs clarification. The reviews use different inclusion sets and measures while overlapping in primary studies (Gaitero et al. 2025; Alves et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No animal study of breastfeeding-related nipple trauma was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols vary. The recent sham-controlled study applied 2 J of 660-nm red light at the nipple and 4 J of 808-nm near-infrared light over the areola, once per breast (Gaitero et al. 2026). Earlier trials used 660-nm laser or near-infrared LEDs around 860 nm, with different energy delivery and schedules (Coca et al. 2016; Camargo et al. 2019; Chaves et al. 2012). No head-to-head trial has established which wavelength, dose, timing, or schedule is best.

Interpretation

Short-term pain relief appears plausible with selected protocols, but its size and duration remain uncertain. Evidence for healing is thinner than the pain evidence. Pain relief and tissue closure should be assessed as separate outcomes in future studies.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The sham-controlled trial supports short-term relief with one protocol, but a modest sample and mixed results leave its size and duration uncertain. The feasibility trial was not designed to evaluate efficacy. One review found an imprecise pain estimate, while a second reported an odds ratio with an invalid negative confidence-limit value. Healing evidence rests on small, mixed studies. Larger trials should assess pain and healing separately (Gaitero et al. 2026; de Paula Leite et al. 2026; Gaitero et al. 2025; Alves et al. 2025).
